Qui est colonisé ? Réflexions autochton: Who Is Colonized? Indigenous Reflections on Colonialism in Quebec
Peut-on dire que les Québécois sont colo: Can it be said that Quebecers are colonized by English speakers? We put the question to Indigenous people.
Gabrielle Paul, Taiaiake et Chris Brown,: Gabrielle Paul, Taiaiake and Chris Brown share their views on Quebec's colonial history.
<strong>« Les Québécois sont un peuple c: “Quebecers are a colonized people.” La Converse discusses Quebec's colonial history and several of its consequences with an Innu, a Cree and a Mohawk.
« Les Québécois sont un peuple colonisé,: “Quebecers are a colonized people, we were colonized by the English.” These words are heard in journalism classes, at academic conferences and from <l1>columnists</l1>. What do Indigenous people living in Quebec have to say about it? On National Indigenous Peoples Day, La Converse discusses Quebec's colonial history and several of its consequences with an Innu, a Cree and a Mohawk.
<strong>« Notre existence leur rappelle: “Our existence constantly reminds them that they're not at home”
Gabrielle Paul est Innue de Mashteuiatsh: Gabrielle Paul is an Innu from Mashteuiatsh, a community that speaks French and Innu-aimun, near Roberval. The young woman is a former journalist for Espaces Autochtones and now works as a policy advisor on government and strategic relations for her band council. Has she heard people tell her that Quebecers are a colonized people, and what does she think of it?
« Oui, c'est un discours qu'on entend fr: “Yes, it's a line we hear often. I think it's something the Quebec political class picks up on a lot. It's often something that comes up, that they can ‘relate’ to what we, Indigenous people, have lived through, because in their heads, since they were colonized by the English, they [think they] can't have done the same thing to us… I can't speak to how Quebecers feel about their history, but that doesn't change the fact that they act, have acted and still act with a colonial attitude,” she tells us in an interview on the eve of National Indigenous Peoples Day.
« Je ne peux pas nier le fait que les Qu: “I can't deny that over the course of history, Quebecers have lived through situations that resemble colonialism in relation to the British Empire. But I can't say it's on the same level as what we, the Indigenous people, have lived through, whether with the British Empire or with the French,” she adds.
Elle estime que la dépossession territor: She believes that the territorial dispossession of Indigenous people by the French is not comparable to the Quebec experience under English domination.
« Tout est lié au territoire. Notre lang: “Everything is tied to the land. Our language is the sounds of the land, and our culture is truly an expression of our way of life on that land. So territorial dispossession is dispossession of everything. In fact, it's probably what bothers Quebecers when we talk about Indigenous people: we are at home, but our existence constantly reminds them that they are not at home, since they took other people's land.”
Taiaiake vit à Kahnawà:ke, la réserve qu: Taiaiake lives in Kahnawà:ke, the reserve along Montréal's South Shore. The Kanienkehà:ka (Mohawk) man is nearing sixty, which shows in his vast knowledge, but the energy that drives him is that of an enthusiastic young university professor. He has been involved in politics since the 1980s. A specialist in Kanien'kehà:ka politics and history, he has published several works on these subjects. In his latest book, It's All about the Land, he tackles racism and settler colonialism. What does this scholar think of the idea that Quebecers were colonized by the English? “I've often heard it in the media and from politicians, but no white Quebecer has dared to say it to me yet,” the historian tells us.
« Je crois que même les plus ardents sou: “I think even the most ardent Quebec sovereignists have to acknowledge that their name is Charlevoix or Fournier, surnames whose roots aren't from here. It comes from somewhere else. It would be very hard for someone to cling to the status of a victim of colonialism when there's an Indigenous person you colonized standing right in front of you.”
Il rappelle que la province a été bâtie: He points out that the province was built on the taking of Indigenous lands. “The fact that people want to preserve and defend the French language in North America, that's beautiful. But you can't use the fact that the French were the first colonizers here, and that they suffered under English domination afterward, to justify, in perpetuity, the erosion of the rights and humanity of everyone else who lives on this territory, which is what Quebec is doing,” adds Taiaiake.
La Converse s'est entretenue avec Chris: La Converse spoke with Chris Brown, a Cree street outreach worker, about his perception of this question. We met him at Atelier Tlachiuak, an art centre that welcomes homeless Indigenous people in Montréal. Chris is from Saskatchewan and has lived in Montréal for about ten years, where he experienced homelessness in the past. The long-haired man, wearing a rock band T-shirt, says he has found more calm with age, which is reflected in the way he speaks. He has never heard a Quebecer describe themselves as “colonized,” but he has heard the expression “pure laine Quebecer,” meaning descendants of the first European arrivals in New France. According to him, however, this expression implies that these “pure laine” Quebecers might have an ancestral right to the land.
« Des francophones disent, “Nous, nous n: “Some francophones say, ‘We weren't the bad guys, the [British] Crown is responsible for all of this!’ But for us, [Indigenous people], it's the same thing. It's a very European way of thinking,” he concludes.
Chris Brown s'est instruit au sujet de l: Chris Brown has educated himself about the philosophy that first justified colonialism in Canada. He believes it is ignored by some Quebecers.
« Je leur demande, “Avez-vous entendu pa: “I ask them, ‘Have you heard of [the Doctrine of Discovery]?’ And they tell me ‘no.’ I explain to them that it's the declaration of the [Catholic] Church saying ‘What we find on these lands, we will keep in the name of God, because it is his will.’ When they find that out, they're pretty shocked. They realize that Canada's history isn't simply based on the signing of treaties.”
<strong>Déclin du français, langues auto: Decline of French, Indigenous languages on the brink of extinction
Le gouvernement Legault a annoncé en avr: Last April, the Legault government announced a <l1>$603-million plan</l1> to “reverse the decline of French in Quebec.” Gabrielle Paul, Chris Brown and Taiaiake fear that these measures and the political and media discourse that accompanies them will overshadow the preservation of Indigenous languages.
<l1>Selon Statistiques Canada</l1>, de 2: <l1>According to Statistics Canada</l1>, from 2016 to 2021, the proportion of Quebecers with French as their mother tongue fell by less than 3% (from 77.1% to 74.8%), and the proportion of Quebecers able to conduct a conversation in French fell by 0.8% (from 94.5% to 93.7%). As for the <l2>70 Indigenous languages spoken in Canada</l2>, all of them are assessed by UNESCO as endangered.
Taiaiake estime que parler de la langue: Taiaiake believes that speaking of the French language as “threatened” is a “rhetorical strategy” on the part of the government. “If [politicians] keep pushing this idea that [francophone Quebecers] are victims and that there's a global force trying to eliminate them, any measure will be justifiable because it will be a matter of self-preservation. When we assume that the French language is threatened with extinction by English speakers or the English language, that's a commonly accepted idea that frees the government from thinking about its decisions in terms of the common good and benefits for society,” he says indignantly.
« Tant et aussi longtemps qu’on pense ça: “As long as people think that, the Quebec government will be able to do whatever it wants and will be supported by people who have been told since childhood that they are victims,” he explains.
Il cite en exemple la<l1> loi 96</l1>. P: He cites <l1>Bill 96</l1> as an example. Passed in 2022, it aims to protect and promote the French language, but also restricts the services available in English. Indigenous leaders criticize the law for causing “<l2>a historic setback</l2>” for reconciliation, particularly for English-speaking First Nations in Quebec that prioritize revitalizing their Indigenous languages. According to APTN, the law has already made postsecondary education <l3>less accessible to Indigenous people</l3>. The cause: the new requirements to give priority to French.
Chris Brown pense qu’il serait préférabl: Chris Brown thinks it would be better to favour a collaborative approach to promoting the French language, and therefore hopes the government will consider the state of Indigenous cultures.
« Je pense qu'ils veulent simplement pro: “I think they simply want to protect [the culture] they had, that they still have. They don't have to protect it so hostilely. I understand that they're losing their language and their culture, but what do you think we [Indigenous people] feel? Because that's what happened to us, so what lessons can we draw from it? It's up to our youth, the next generations coming up, to fix all of this,” he says.
Pourtant, Chris Brown a décidé d'apprend: Still, Chris Brown decided to learn to speak French in order to take part more easily in Quebec society.
« Il est essentiel au Québec de parler f: “It's essential to speak French in Quebec. Before, I was very resistant to learning it. I didn't want to speak it. But it was mostly youthful ignorance. As I got older, I understood that I needed this language to talk with a lot of people. Without it, I lost several opportunities, even the possibility of friendships with certain people. So I spend more time with francophones and I practise the language,” he explains.
Taiaiake préfère, lui, parler en anglais: Taiaiake, for his part, prefers to speak English. Although he acknowledges that the government has granted a few exceptions for Indigenous people as part of its French-language preservation measures, he thinks that on the ground, Quebecers are not accommodating toward those who don't speak their language.
« Tout le monde sait que vivre dans la r: “Everyone knows that living in the Montréal area means facing an aggressive francophone environment. There is very little tolerance in Quebec for people who don't speak French. And not only those who don't speak French, but those who don't speak French according to their standards,” he says.
Gabrielle Paul, qui parle français, esti: Gabrielle Paul, who speaks French, believes that her command of the language doesn't always make communication with non-Indigenous Quebecers easier.
« Même si on parle la même langue, bien,: “Even if we speak the same language, well, we have ways of seeing the world that aren't compatible,” she notes. She believes that many Quebecers are not open to Indigenous knowledge, to the differences that show up particularly in politics, for example on the importance of the collective or the notion of private land.
Elle regrette l'attitude « paternaliste: She regrets the “paternalistic” attitude of the Quebec government toward First Nations. “You can see it in the discussions we have with the Quebec government, this idea of superiority comes up all the time because they're always trying to impose their way of doing things, impose their vision, make sure that Quebec laws can always apply on our territory. On the question of self-determination, they're not there at all.”
Ces réflexions nous ont été confiées que: These reflections were shared with us a few days before National Indigenous Peoples Day. A great opportunity to come together, say Taiaiake, Gabrielle and Chris, who nonetheless express a few reservations.
« Je n'ai pas vraiment besoin d'une jour: “I don't really need a special day to celebrate with my friends. Every day is Indigenous Peoples Day for me. But it's nice, I guess, to have a special day for us nationally,” acknowledges Chris Brown.
Taiaiake, quant à lui, pense que la jour: Taiaiake, for his part, thinks the day is too superficial to truly celebrate Indigenous people.
« Je pense que [la Journée nationale des: “I think [National Indigenous Peoples Day] would be important if all Indigenous people had the day off, if it were a statutory holiday to acknowledge the injustices and the colonialism inflicted on our cultures, our nations and our lands. But I find that the way it's presented as a national event is too much like a celebration of our assimilation into the broader culture of Canada,” he adds.
Gabrielle Paul pense aussi qu'il devrait: Gabrielle Paul also thinks there should be greater awareness-raising among non-Indigenous people on that day. “It should be a day of awareness for everyone, you know, to see and acknowledge Indigenous cultures. But you know, I feel like it's really more us, Indigenous people, who celebrate, not at the national level.”
Malgré l’absence de reconnaissance du co: Despite the failure of some Quebecers to acknowledge colonialism in la belle province, Taiaiake, Gabrielle and Chris sense that this attitude is becoming less and less common among young people.
Taiaiake remarque que les jeunes Québéco: Taiaiake notes that young Quebecers show greater openness toward the history of their country and challenge the idea that they are a colonized people.
« L’idée selon laquelle ils auraient été: “The idea that they were colonized has evolved, now we refer more to marginalization or oppression experienced within a capitalist society. An oppression caused by the economically and politically dominant group, which identifies as English-speaking. I recognize that, and I think many people recognize it too. Younger generations are sensitive to it, they think it's unfair, this power imbalance [between francophones and anglophones],” says Taiaiake.
Chris Brown dit avoir rencontré des amis: Chris Brown says he has met non-Indigenous friends who are more open-minded.
« Beaucoup de mes amis disent “Nous somm: “A lot of my friends say, ‘We're sorry your lands were stolen. It wasn't us, it was our ancestors.’ I think younger generations are more and more open-minded about the hardships we've faced with colonialism. And I hope that in a few years, there won't be such a big divide between the French, the English and Indigenous people,” he muses.
Pour réellement avancer, Gabrielle Paul: To truly move forward, Gabrielle Paul advocates recognizing the colonial dynamics still at work: “The fact that colonialism isn't something in the past, that it's something that continues over time and is repeated, like. I think the public could really understand our issues better if that were really better grasped.”
